subject: Climate & Environment
title: Shells That Dissolve
description: A short lesson to help you apply Shells That Dissolve.

hook.text: Oyster larvae in Oregon started dying mysteriously in 2007. The culprit was acidified water.

buildup.text: Many marine creatures build shells from calcium carbonate — the same compound in chalk.

discovery.text: Acidic water dissolves calcium carbonate. Shells and skeletons become thinner and weaker.

twist.text: Pteropods — tiny sea snails — are already showing dissolving shells in Antarctic waters.

climax.text: These creatures are food for salmon, whales, and seabirds. Their loss ripples up the food chain.

punchline.text: The ocean is dissolving the armor of its smallest creatures.

quiz.question: What does ocean acidification do to shells?
options: Dissolves calcium carbonate, making shells thinner

details.summary: Shellfish, sea urchins, and tiny pteropods build protective shells from calcium carbonate. As ocean pH drops, the water becomes corrosive to these minerals, literally dissolving the shells of living organisms. Pteropod shell thinning has already been observed in the Southern Ocean.
details.whyItMatters: Pteropods are a critical food source for fish, whales, and seabirds. Shell dissolution at the base of the food web could cascade upward, affecting entire marine ecosystems and fisheries.
takeaways: Acidic water dissolves the calcium carbonate in shells
Pteropod shell thinning is already observed in polar waters
Shell loss cascades up the food web to fish and seabirds

faq.question: Why are pteropods so important?
faq.answer: Pteropods are tiny swimming snails that form a major food source for juvenile salmon, herring, and baleen whales in polar and subpolar waters. Their decline could ripple through the food web, reducing fish stocks and affecting larger predators.

faq.question: At what pH do shells start dissolving?
faq.answer: Aragonite, the mineral many shells are made of, begins to dissolve when ocean pH falls below about 7.8 at the surface. Some deep and polar waters already reach these levels. Projections suggest widespread surface undersaturation by 2100 under high emissions.
